## 2. Per-Language Semantic Sketch

### Georgian (ka)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Georgian distinguishes factual correctness (სწორი sts'ori, მართალი mart'ali), authenticity/genuineness (ნამდვილი namdvili, ჭეშმარიტი ch'eshmarit'i), deliberate lying (ტყუილი t'q'uili, მოტყუება mot'q'ueba), sincerity (გულწრფელი gults'rpeli), reliability (სანდო sando), moral justice (სამართლიანი samart'liani), and appearance vs. reality (მოჩვენებითი moch'venebiti, ზედაპირული zedap'iruli). The root mart'l- is notably polysemous, spanning factual correctness, moral rightness, legal justice, and orthographic correctness. ნამდვილი namdvili participates in at least four semantic groups (authenticity, emotional genuineness, reality vs. appearance, fiction vs. fact). ტყუილი t'q'uili has an unusual semantic extension from "lie" to "in vain/futile."

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** The mart'l- root generates an exceptionally large derivational family including legal terms (სამართალი samart'ali "law"), directional terms (მართლწერა mart'lts'era "orthography"), religious terms (მართლმადიდებელი mart'lmadidebeli "Orthodox"), and modal verbs (მართებს mart'ebs "it befits"). The negative prefix უ- (u-) creates privative forms (უტყუარი ut'q'uari "infallible," უსამართლობა usamart'loba "injustice"). The abstract noun suffixes სი-...-ე (si-...-e) and -ობა (-oba) are both productive.

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Georgian shows a rich set of evidential particles (თურმე turme, ხომ khom, მეთქი metki) that mark epistemic stance. The contrastive frame არა X, არამედ Y (ara X, aramed Y) is a fixed correction construction. Concessive constructions (მართალია, მაგრამ... mart'alia, magram...) are well-attested. Causative morphology for truth predicates is marginal; lexical verbs (დაამტკიცა daamt'k'itsa "proved") are preferred.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** Georgian shows both lexical oppositions (სიმართლე/ტყუილი, ნამდვილი/ყალბი, ბუნებრივი/ხელოვნური) and morphological oppositions via negative prefixes (უ-, არა-). Several constructional oppositions use the same noun modified by contrasting adjectives (სანდო წყარო vs. საეჭვო წყარო). Asymmetries include the absence of a fixed lexical opposite for ნაღდი ფული "cash" and the absence of a symmetric lexicalization for "unconvincing evidence."

### Yoruba (yo)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Yoruba organizes the truth domain around a small set of core roots: tọ́ (to be straight/correct), irọ́/purọ́ (lie/to lie), bá mu (to correspond/match), jọ (to resemble), dájú (to be certain), gbàgbọ́ (to believe), yẹ (to be fitting), and gidi (genuine). The root tọ́ spans factual correctness, moral character, appropriateness, and directional metaphors (ọ̀nà tọ́ "straight path"). Correspondence and matching (bá mu, ìbámu) form a distinct cluster. Genuineness (gidi) lacks a specific lexical antonym; negation is used instead. The domain of investigation and verification is expressed through a large set of ṣe + noun constructions.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** The nominalization prefix ì- is highly productive (ìgbàgbọ́, ìdájú, ìbámu, ìmọ̀). The negative nominalizer àì- creates privative abstract nouns (àìtọ́, àìmọ̀, àìbámu, àìyẹ, àìpé). The agentive prefix a- creates apurọ́ "liar" but does not productively apply to tọ́ (*atọ́ is not attested). "Truthful person" requires the compound ọmọ òtítọ́ (child of truth) rather than a morphological agentive. The gerundive prefix gbí-/pí-/ṣí- creates action nouns.

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Yoruba treats truth as a static, categorical property: inchoative constructions ("becoming true") are marginal or reinterpreted as discovery/revelation. Causative constructions for truth states are pragmatically odd (one cannot "make" truth); causing belief (mú kí n gbàgbọ́) is natural, but causing truth (mú kí ó tọ́) is reinterpreted as verification. Serial verb constructions (fi...hàn, bá...mu) are central. The focus construction with ni is highly productive for emphatic truth assertion. Proverbial constructions (Noun + á + Verb + Noun) carry cultural authority.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The primary opposition is òtítọ́/irọ́ (truth/lie) and tọ́/purọ́ (be correct/lie). Morphological negation with kò is the standard strategy for most oppositions. A notable constructional asymmetry: sọ òtítọ́ (speak truth) uses sọ while pa irọ́ (tell a lie) uses pa (conventionalized), creating an asymmetric verb pairing. The ọmọ òtítọ́/apurọ́ opposition shows agentive asymmetry (compound vs. prefix). Degree modification of truth predicates is resisted (truth is conceptualized as binary).

### Finnish (fi)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Finnish distinguishes factual correspondence (tosi, totuus, paikkansapitävä, todenmukainen), correctness evaluation (oikea, oikeellinen, väärä, virheellinen), authenticity (aito, aitous), deception and falsification (valhe, valehdella, väärentää, vääristää, harhaanjohtava), honesty and sincerity (rehellinen, vilpitön), evidential and proof terms (todistaa, todiste, todistaja), reliability (luotettava, uskottava), probability (todennäköinen), realization and actualization (toteutua, todellistua, toteuttaa), and real-life versus fiction (tosielämä, tositarina). The tosi- root is exceptionally productive, generating compounds (tosiasia, tosielämä, tosi-tv) and grammaticalized adverbials (totta kai, totta puhuen). The väärä- root spans incorrectness, falsification, forgery, misuse, and physical abnormality.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** Finnish shows highly productive abstract nominalization (-uus/-yys, -suus/-syys), agentive nominalization (-ja/-jä), gerund formation (-minen), result noun formation (-e, -us, -os), and causative/inchoative pairs (todellistaa/todellistua, toteuttaa/toteutua). The privative suffix -tön/-ttömyys is productive (vilpitön "sincere," literally "without deceit"). The negative prefix epä- creates antonyms (epätosi, epärehellinen, epätodennäköinen). Spatial/directional uses of oikea (right-hand) and väärä (physical abnormality) represent semantic divergence from the truth domain.

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Finnish shows a notable gap: no simple inchoative for "becoming false/untrue" — the concept is expressed through discovery constructions (osoittautua vääräksi "turn out to be false," paljastua valheeksi "be revealed as a lie"). The fixed inessive constructions olla oikeassa/olla väärässä (to be right/wrong) are grammaticalized spatial metaphors. Translative case constructions (todistettiin vääräksi "was proven false") are productive. The adverb totta kai "of course" is fully grammaticalized. Finnish lacks a simple causative "make genuine" (*aitouttaa not attested).

**Oppositional structures (F5):** Finnish shows both lexical (tosi/väärä, totuus/valhe, aito/väärennös) and morphological (epä- prefix, -tön privative) oppositions. Several asymmetries are noted: väärinkäsitys "misunderstanding" is lexicalized but oikea käsitys "correct understanding" is not; väärinkäyttö "misuse" is lexicalized but oikea käyttö "proper use" is not. The opposition valehdella/puhua totuutta is asymmetric (dedicated verb for lying vs. verb+object construction for truth-telling). Several implied oppositions (tosielämä/fiktio, tositarina/satutarina) lack lexicalized antonyms in the data.

### Basque (eu)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Basque distinguishes truth-stating and verification (egia, egiazkoa, egiaztatu, ziurra), authenticity and genuineness (benetakoa, egiazko maitasuna), falsehood and deception (gezurra, gezurrezko, iruzurra, faltsua), correctness and error (zuzena, okerra, zehatza), reliability and credibility (fidagarria, sinesgarria, zalantzagarria), moral honesty (zintzoa), similarity and identity (berdina, antzekoa), appearance and manifestation (itxurazko, ageria), directness (zuzenean, zuzeneko), and legal/administrative validation (zuzenbide, egiaztagiri, ziurtagiri). The zuzen- root spans physical straightness, factual correctness, moral rightness, legal concepts (zuzenbide "law"), organizational direction (zuzendari "director"), and live broadcasting (zuzenean "live").

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** The -tasun abstract noun suffix is highly productive (egiazkotasuna, zuzentasuna, berdintasuna, zehaztasuna, zintzotasuna). The verbalizing suffixes -tu and -zta- create causative/factitive verbs (egiaztatu, ziurtatu, zuzendu, zehaztu). The -garri suffix creates evaluative adjectives (fidagarria, sinesgarria, zalantzagarria, frogagarria). The -keria suffix creates pejorative collective nouns (gezurkeria, faltsukeria, iruzurkeria). Reduplication is used for emphasis (gezur-gezurra, zuzen-zuzen, berdin-berdin, ziur-ziur).

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Basque uses bihurtu (become) for inchoative constructions, but specialized verbs (egiaztatu, okertu, agertu) are preferred. The locative constructions agerian jarri/egon (expose/be exposed) and zalantzan jarri/egon (call into question/be in doubt) are highly productive parallel patterns. Modal necessity with behar (must) is common. The -garri suffix creates a productive class of evaluative adjectives. Binomial expressions (egia eta gezurra, zuzen eta oker) are fixed with positive term first.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** Basque shows lexical (egia/gezurra, zuzena/okerra, zintzoa/faltsua), morphological (egiaztatu/gezurtatu, zuzendu/okertu, zuzentasuna/okertasuna), and constructional (egia esan/gezurra esan, zuzen egin/oker egin, agerian jarri/ezkutatu) oppositions. Moral asymmetry in nominalization: zintzotasuna uses neutral -tasun while faltsukeria uses pejorative -keria. The implied oppositions sinesgarria/sinesgaitza and frogagarria/frogaezina use different suffixes (-garri vs. -gaitz/-ezin) rather than negation.

### Tamil (ta)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Tamil has two major truth roots distributed by register: uṇmai (general, all registers) and mey (literary, classical, philosophical/spiritual). Both contrast with poy (lie/falsehood). Additional distinctions include factual correctness (cari, tappu/tavaṟu), moral rightness (nērmai, niyāyam, aṟam, nīti), authenticity (pōli "fake," acal "original"), reliability (nampakam, nampikkai), possibility (cāttiyam), doubt (cantēkam), certainty (uṟuti), clarity (teḷivu), appropriateness (poruttam), and natural state/essence (iyalpu). The mey root generates an extensive cluster of philosophical and spiritual compounds (meyññāṉam, meyyanpu, mey teyvam, mey pakti) that are absent for uṇmai.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** The -āṉa adjectival suffix and -āka adverbial suffix are universally productive across all truth-domain bases. The negative adjectival suffix -aṟṟa (without) creates privative adjectives (uṇmaiyaṟṟa, nērmaiyaṟṟa, niyāyamaṟṟa, poruttamaṟṟa). The abstract noun suffix -taṉmai (quality/nature) creates formal quality nouns (uṇmaittaṉmai, poyttaṉmai). Agentive nominalization is restricted: poyyan/poyyāḷ/poyyar (liar) exists for poy but no parallel *uṇmaiyaṉ (truth-teller) is attested; truth-tellers require periphrastic expression.

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Tamil shows a strong preference for verb+object collocations (uṇmaiyai col, poy col) with an asymmetry: uṇmai takes the accusative marker -ai while poy appears without case marking in the standard collocation. Inchoative constructions are productive (uṇmai āku, poy ampalamāku). Causative constructions use -paṭuttu (teḷivupaṭuttu "clarify," uṟutipaṭuttu "confirm"). Emphatic particle stacking (-il-ē-y-ē) is characteristic of Tamil. Degree modification of truth predicates is marginal (truth treated as categorical). Reciprocal, benefactive, and instrumental constructions with truth-domain terms are absent or unattested.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The primary lexical opposition is uṇmai/poy and mey/poy. The -aṟṟa suffix creates systematic morphological oppositions (uṇmaiyāṉa/uṇmaiyaṟṟa, nērmaiyāṉa/nērmaiyaṟṟa). Contrastive disjunction constructions (uṇmaiyā poyyā "true or false?", cariyā tappā "right or wrong?") are highly productive. Register stratification creates a three-way opposition: uṇmai (general), mey (literary/classical), nijam (colloquial). The agentive asymmetry (poyyar "liars" vs. no lexicalized "truth-teller") parallels patterns in other languages.

### Indonesian (id)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Indonesian distinguishes factual correctness (benar, betul, salah, keliru), authenticity of objects (asli, palsu, tulen), legal/procedural validity (sah, absah, batal, valid, sahih), existence and reality (nyata, kenyataan, sejati, sungguh, hakikat), deliberate deception (bohong, dusta), honesty (jujur), precision (tepat, akurat, pas), similarity (sama, mirip), appropriateness (cocok, wajar, pantas), and error attribution (salah, kesalahan, menyalahkan). The benar root is exceptionally broad, spanning factual truth, moral rightness, procedural correctness, and general affirmation. The salah root spans incorrectness, moral wrongness, blame attribution, and grammaticalized uses (salah satu "one of").

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** Indonesian shows highly productive prefix/suffix combinations: meN-...-kan (causative transitive), di-...-kan (passive), ke-...-an (abstract nominalization), peN-...-an (action nominalization), ber- (stative/intransitive), ter- (accidental/resultative). The ter- prefix creates evidential/discovery forms (ternyata "it turns out," tersalah "accidentally wrong"). Reduplication creates intensifiers (benar-benar, betul-betul, sungguh-sungguh) and colloquial forms (bohong-bohongan "pretend/fake"). The compound penyalahgunaan "abuse/misuse" shows productive compounding of salah with guna.

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Indonesian shows a notable gap: no dedicated construction for "prove false" — this requires circumlocution. Positive character causation ("make someone honest") is also absent as a productive pattern. The evidential ternyata is fully grammaticalized. The discourse markers sebenarnya, sesungguhnya, sebetulnya function as truth-framing adverbials. The hedging construction kurang + adjective (kurang tepat "not quite right") is a productive politeness strategy. Inchoative menjadi constructions are natural for most truth-domain terms.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** Indonesian shows lexical (benar/salah, asli/palsu, jujur/bohong, sah/batal), morphological (tidak + adjective as universal negation strategy), and constructional oppositions. Several asymmetries: väärinkäsitys-type compounds (väärinkäsitys, väärinkäyttö) are lexicalized while their positive counterparts are not. sejati and tulen lack clear lexical antonyms. The opposition hakikat vs. (surface appearance) is conceptual rather than lexically encoded.

### Turkish (tr)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Turkish distinguishes factual correctness (doğru, yanlış, hatalı, isabetli), reality and authenticity (gerçek, sahte, asıl, özgün, taklit, doğal, yapay), trustworthiness (güvenilir, sağlam, tutarlı, inandırıcı), honesty and moral character (dürüst, yalancı), deception (yanıltıcı, yalan), doubt and suspicion (şüpheli, kuşkulu), certainty (kesin, şüphesiz), rights, justice, and fairness (hak, haklı, haksız, adil, adalet, meşru), validity and legitimacy (geçerli, meşru), and fundamental/elevated truth (hakikat, hakiki). The hak root (from Arabic ḥaqq) is notably polysemous, spanning rights, justice, truth, and religious reference (Allah hakkı için). The doğru root spans factual truth, spatial directness, and moral rightness.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** Turkish shows highly productive inchoative (-leş-) and causative (-leştir-) pairs (gerçekleşmek/gerçekleştirmek, kesinleşmek/kesinleştirmek, meşrulaşmak/meşrulaştırmak). The abstract nominalizer -luk/-lük is universally productive. The privative suffix -sız/-siz creates antonyms (haksız, şüphesiz, hatasız, güvenilmez). The agentive suffix -cı/-ci creates adherent/practitioner nouns (gerçekçi "realist," yalancı "liar," sahtekâr "fraud"). The Arabic-origin suffix -kâr (sahtekâr) and -iyet (meşruiyet, hakkaniyet) appear in formal/elevated vocabulary.

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Turkish shows productive resultative constructions with çıkmak (doğru çıkmak "turn out to be true," yanlış çıkmak "turn out to be wrong," haklı çıkmak "be proven right"). The light verb constructions with etmek, olmak, and söylemek are central. Idiomatic expressions using body/spatial metaphors (gerçek yüz "true face," doğru yol "right path") are well-attested. The hak-based idioms (hak vermek, hak yemek, hakkını vermek) form a rich cluster. Causative morphology for truth predicates is productive (doğrulamak, yanlışlamak, yalanlamak).

**Oppositional structures (F5):** Turkish shows lexical (doğru/yanlış, gerçek/sahte, haklı/haksız, dürüst/yalancı), morphological (privative -sız: şüphesiz, hatasız; negative prefix: güvenilmez), and constructional (doğru çıkmak/yanlış çıkmak, haklı çıkmak/haksız çıkmak) oppositions. The acı gerçek/tatlı yalan (bitter truth/sweet lie) opposition uses taste metaphors. Several items lack clear lexical antonyms (sejati-type: hakikat lacks a simple opposite). The hakkında postposition is fully grammaticalized from the hak root.

### Korean (ko)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Korean distinguishes factual correspondence (진실 jinsil, 사실 sasil, 실제 silje), deliberate deception (거짓 geojit, 거짓말 geojinmal, 허위 heowi), authenticity of objects (진짜 jinjja, 가짜 gajja, 진본 jinbon, 모조 mojo), honest character (정직 jeongjik, 솔직 soljik, 진심 jinsim), correctness evaluation (맞다 matda, 틀리다 teullida, 옳다 olda), legitimacy and justification (정당하다 jeongdanghada, 타당하다 tadanghada), credibility (신빙성 sinbingseong, 그럴듯하다 geureoldeuthada), certainty (확실하다 hwaksilhada, 명백하다 myeongbaekhada), and practical reality (실제 silje, 실질 siljil, 실천 silcheon, 실현 silhyeon). The 진 (jin) morpheme appears in truth/genuineness compounds, advancement/progress compounds, medical examination terms, and calming contexts — representing either polysemy or homophony. The 실 (sil) morpheme generates an extensive cluster of practical reality terms.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries (F2a):** Sino-Korean negative prefixes 부- (bu-) and 불- (bul-) are productive for formal negation (부정직, 부정확, 불확실). The abstract quality suffix -성 (-seong) is highly productive with Sino-Korean bases (정확성, 타당성, 신빙성, 확실성). The adverbial suffix -히 (-hi) and the adverbial construction -하게 (-hage) are both productive. Agentive nominalization is asymmetric: 거짓말쟁이 "liar" exists but no parallel "truth-teller" agentive is attested; truth-tellers require periphrastic expression.

**Constructional patterns and absences (F4):** Korean shows a notable resistance to simple inchoative and causative constructions for truth predicates: "becoming true/false" for propositions is marginal, and "making something true" has no productive pattern. Truth emergence is expressed through specialized verbs (드러나다 deureonada "come to light," 밝혀지다 balkhyeojida "be brought to light"). Causation of truth states is expressed periphrastically (-게 하다 construction). The discourse markers 사실은 (sasireun) "actually" and 솔직히 (soljiki) "frankly" are grammaticalized. Evidential marking with 것 같다 (geot gatda) is highly productive.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** Korean shows lexical (진실/거짓, 진짜/가짜, 맞다/틀리다, 옳다/그르다), morphological (부-/불- prefixes, -지 않다 negation), and constructional (진실을 밝히다/진실을 숨기다, 신빙성이 있다/없다) oppositions. The agentive asymmetry (거짓말쟁이 "liar" vs. no lexicalized "truth-teller") is notable. 그르다 "to be wrong" is archaic, surviving mainly in the fixed expression 옳고 그름. Several items (명백하다, 그럴듯하다, 사실상) lack clear lexical antonyms in the data.

## 3. Cross-Language Summary

### Recurring Convergences (patterns observed across many languages)

- **Lexical separation of deliberate lying from factual error.** All eight languages maintain a distinction between terms for deliberate falsehood/deception (Georgian ტყუილი, Yoruba irọ́/purọ́, Finnish valhe, Basque gezurra, Tamil poy, Indonesian bohong, Turkish yalan, Korean 거짓말) and terms for unintentional error or incorrectness (Georgian მცდარი, Yoruba àṣìṣe, Finnish virheellinen, Basque okerra, Tamil tappu/tavaṟu, Indonesian keliru, Turkish hatalı, Korean 틀리다). The deception terms consistently carry stronger moral valence.

- **Agentive nominalization asymmetry: "liar" is lexicalized; "truth-teller" is not.** Across at least six languages, a dedicated agentive noun for "liar" or "habitual liar" exists (Georgian მატყუარა, Yoruba apurọ́, Finnish valehtelija, Basque gezurlari, Tamil poyyan/poyyar, Indonesian pembohong, Turkish yalancı, Korean 거짓말쟁이), while a parallel agentive for "truth-teller" is either absent or requires periphrastic expression. This asymmetry is observed in Georgian, Yoruba, Finnish, Tamil, Indonesian, and Korean explicitly; it is implied in Basque and Turkish.

- **Productive abstract nominalization from truth-domain adjectives.** All languages show productive patterns for deriving abstract quality nouns from truth-domain bases: Georgian -ობა/-ება, Yoruba ì- prefix, Finnish -uus/-yys, Basque -tasun, Tamil -taṉmai, Indonesian ke-...-an, Turkish -luk/-lük, Korean -성 (-seong). These nominalizations are used in formal, philosophical, and analytical discourse.

- **Discourse markers derived from truth-domain roots.** In all eight languages, truth-domain items have grammaticalized into discourse markers that introduce corrections, frank statements, or factual clarifications: Georgian მართლაც (mart'lats) "really, indeed," Yoruba nitootọ́ "truly," Finnish sebenarnya/totta puhuen, Basque benetan "truly, really," Tamil uṇmaiyil "in truth, actually," Indonesian sebenarnya "actually, in fact," Turkish gerçekten "really, truly," Korean 사실은 (sasireun) "actually, in fact" and 솔직히 (soljiki) "frankly." This grammaticalization pattern is cross-linguistically robust.

- **Resistance to degree modification of core truth predicates.** Multiple languages show that core truth predicates resist scalar or degree modification. Yoruba explicitly treats tọ́ as binary and non-gradable; Korean data notes that truth predicates resist degree modification; Finnish shows that truth-becoming constructions are conceptualized as discrete events rather than gradual processes; Basque and Tamil show similar patterns. This contrasts with related terms like "credibility" or "similarity," which are freely gradable in all languages.

- **Separation of authenticity/genuineness from factual truth.** All languages maintain a distinction between terms evaluating the truth-value of statements and terms evaluating the genuineness or authenticity of objects, persons, or emotions. Georgian distinguishes ჭეშმარიტი (true statements) from ნამდვილი (genuine things); Yoruba distinguishes tọ́ (correct) from gidi (genuine); Finnish distinguishes tosi (true) from aito (genuine); Basque distinguishes egia (truth) from benetakoa (genuine); Tamil distinguishes uṇmai (truth) from acal (original/genuine); Indonesian distinguishes benar (correct) from asli (authentic); Turkish distinguishes doğru (correct) from gerçek (real/genuine); Korean distinguishes 진실 (truth) from 진짜 (genuine/real).

- **Proverbial or idiomatic expressions asserting the ultimate triumph or difficulty of truth.** All eight languages show fixed or semi-fixed expressions asserting that truth will eventually be revealed or that lies are short-lived: Georgian "ტყუილს მოკლე ფეხები აქვს" (lies have short legs), Yoruba "òtítọ́ á kọjá irọ́" (truth will surpass lies), Finnish "totuus paljastuu lopulta" (truth will be revealed eventually), Basque "egia eta gezurra" binomial, Tamil "uṇmai iṟutiyil vellum" (truth will triumph in the end), Indonesian "ternyata benar" (it turns out to be true), Turkish "acı gerçek" (bitter truth), Korean "진실은 언제나 밝혀진다" (the truth always comes to light). These expressions reflect a shared cultural framing of truth as something that persists or emerges despite concealment.

---

### Major Divergences (patterns observed in only a few languages or showing strong contrast)

- **Extent of a single root's semantic range.** Georgian mart'l- and Turkish hak- show unusually wide semantic extension: mart'l- covers factual correctness, moral rightness, legal justice, orthography, religious denomination, and modal propriety; hak- covers rights, justice, truth, religious reference, and grammaticalized postposition. By contrast, Yoruba tọ́ and Korean 맞다 (matda) have narrower, more focused ranges. Finnish tosi- and Indonesian benar show intermediate breadth.

- **Presence of a distinct register-stratified truth vocabulary.** Tamil is the most clearly documented case of register stratification within the truth domain: uṇmai (general), mey (literary/classical/spiritual), and nijam (colloquial/borrowed) are distributed across registers with different collocational patterns. Korean shows a Sino-Korean vs. native Korean stratum (진실 vs. 참) but less elaborately. Georgian, Finnish, and Turkish show formal/informal variation but not a three-way register split of this kind.

- **Semantic extension of "lie/false" to "futile/in vain."** Georgian ტყუილი (t'q'uili) has a well-documented extension from "lie" to "in vain, for nothing" (ტყუილად "in vain," ტყუილუბრალოდ "pointlessly"). This semantic extension is not documented in the other seven languages, where "lie" terms remain within the deception domain.

- **Elaboration of a practical reality vs. theory distinction.** Korean shows the most extensive vocabulary for distinguishing actual practice from theory or nominal status, with a large cluster of 실- (sil-) compounds (실제, 실질, 실천, 실행, 실현, 실력, 실적, 실효, 실무, 실전, 실습, 실험, 실시간, etc.). Indonesian shows a similar but less extensive pattern (nyata, kenyataan, faktual). The other languages do not show this degree of lexical elaboration in this specific domain.

- **Elaboration of rights and justice vocabulary within the truth domain.** Turkish shows the most extensive development of hak-based vocabulary (haklı, haksız, hakkaniyet, hakketmek, hak vermek, hak yemek, hakkını almak, hakkını helal etmek, hak sahibi, hak iddia etmek, hak aramak, hak ve adalet, etc.) as part of the broader truth/correctness domain. Georgian also shows significant development of the mart'l-/samart'l- cluster for justice and law. Yoruba òdodo (justice/righteousness) and Korean 정당하다 (legitimacy) participate in this domain but with less elaboration.

- **Resistance to inchoative and causative constructions for truth predicates.** Yoruba and Korean show the strongest documented resistance to inchoative ("become true/false") and causative ("make true/false") constructions for propositional truth. Both languages reinterpret such constructions as discovery/revelation or verification rather than change in truth-value. Finnish shows a partial gap (no common expression for "become untrue"). Georgian, Turkish, and Indonesian show more productive inchoative and causative patterns in this domain.

- **Elaboration of legal and administrative validation vocabulary.** Finnish shows the most extensive cluster of evidential and proof terms (todistaa, todiste, todistaja, todistus, todistusaineisto, todistustaakka, todistuskappale, todistettava, todistettavasti, todentaa, todentaminen). Basque shows a parallel cluster (egiaztagiri, ziurtagiri, egiaztapen, egiaztatze). Georgian and Korean show legal vocabulary but less systematically organized. Yoruba and Tamil show less elaboration in this specific sub-domain.

---

### Asymmetries, Gaps, and Irregularities

- **Asymmetric lexicalization of negative vs. positive poles.** Across multiple languages, the negative pole (falsehood, error, inauthenticity) is more lexically elaborated or differently structured than the positive pole. Finnish väärinkäsitys "misunderstanding" and väärinkäyttö "misuse" are lexicalized while their positive counterparts are not. Indonesian shows the same pattern. Korean 거짓말쟁이 "liar" is lexicalized while "truth-teller" is not. Yoruba apurọ́ "liar" uses the agentive prefix while ọmọ òtítọ́ "truthful person" requires a compound. This asymmetry is observed in at least six of the eight languages.

- **Morphological homophony or polysemy creating cross-domain extension.** Several languages show a single morpheme spanning the truth domain and unrelated domains. Georgian mart'l- extends to orthography and religious denomination. Turkish hak- extends to rights and religious reference. Korean 진 (jin) appears in truth/genuineness, advancement/progress, medical examination, and calming contexts. Basque zuzen- extends to organizational direction and live broadcasting. Finnish oikea extends to spatial direction (right-hand side). These extensions are language-specific and do not show a common cross-linguistic pattern.

- **Absence of a simple verb meaning "to tell the truth" parallel to "to lie."** In several languages, lying has a dedicated verb while truth-telling requires a verb+object construction. Finnish has valehdella "to lie" but no *totuudella; Yoruba has purọ́ "to lie" but sọ òtítọ́ (speak + truth) for truth-telling; Korean has 거짓말하다 (geojinmalhada) "to lie" but 진실을 말하다 (jinsireul malhada) for truth-telling; Tamil has poy col (lie + say) vs. uṇmaiyai col (truth + say). This asymmetry is observed in at least four languages and implied in others.

- **Variation in how "correspondence" or "matching" is lexicalized.** Yoruba has a dedicated cluster for correspondence and matching (bá mu, ìbámu, jọ, ìjọra) that is more elaborated than in other languages. Georgian has ადეკვატური (adek'vat'uri) and მსგავსი (msgavsi) but these are borrowed or less central. Finnish, Turkish, and Indonesian have terms for similarity (mirip, sama, mirip) but not a dedicated correspondence cluster. This suggests Yoruba has developed a more explicit vocabulary for the correspondence relation between representations and reality.

- **Variation in the treatment of objectivity/subjectivity as a distinct semantic domain.** Georgian explicitly includes ობიექტური (obiek't'uri) and სუბიექტური (subiek't'uri) as a distinct semantic group (Group 8 in F3). These are borrowed terms present in all languages but only Georgian's F3 analysis identifies them as forming a distinct semantic cluster. This may reflect analytical choices in the F3 tables rather than a genuine cross-linguistic difference, but it is the only language where this distinction is explicitly grouped.

- **Variation in the elaboration of "appearance vs. reality" vocabulary.** Georgian, Basque, and Turkish show the most explicit vocabulary for distinguishing surface appearance from underlying reality (Georgian მოჩვენებითი moch'venebiti, ზედაპირული zedap'iruli, ნამდვილი სახე namdvili sakhe; Basque itxurazko, ageria, funtsean; Turkish gerçek yüz, gerçeğe aykırı, gerçekdışı). Korean 진면목 (jinmyeonmok) "true character" and Tamil uṇmai mukam "true face" show parallel metaphors but less systematic elaboration. Yoruba and Indonesian show this distinction but with less dedicated vocabulary.

- **Presence of taste or color metaphors for truth and lies.** Turkish acı gerçek (bitter truth) and tatlı yalan (sweet lie) use taste metaphors. Korean 새빨간 거짓말 (bright red lie) uses a color metaphor. Georgian ტყუილი (t'q'uili) has the proverb "ტყუილს მოკლე ფეხები აქვს" (lies have short legs) using a body metaphor. Yoruba "òtítọ́ korò" (truth is bitter) also uses a taste metaphor. These metaphorical extensions are present in multiple languages but the specific metaphors differ; taste metaphors for truth/lies appear in at least three languages (Turkish, Yoruba, and implied in Korean's white lie calque).

## Narrative Analysis

### Recurring Partition Patterns

**The factual correctness / deliberate deception split is universal.** Every language in the dataset maintains a lexical distinction between terms evaluating whether statements correspond to facts and terms marking intentional false representation. The deception terms consistently carry stronger moral valence and tend to be more lexically elaborated on the negative pole (liars are named; truth-tellers are not). This split is not merely a matter of having separate words: the two domains show different constructional behavior, different collocational patterns, and different derivational productivity across all eight languages.

**The authenticity/genuineness domain is universally present but variably organized.** All eight languages distinguish terms for genuine, original, or authentic objects from terms for fakes, counterfeits, or imitations. However, the relationship between this domain and the factual truth domain varies. In Georgian, ნამდვილი (namdvili) participates in both authenticity and factual truth contexts. In Finnish, aito (genuine) is kept more separate from tosi (true). In Indonesian, asli (authentic) and benar (correct) are clearly distinct. In Yoruba, gidi (genuine) is a separate item from tọ́ (correct). The degree of overlap between "genuine object" and "true statement" vocabulary is a point of cross-language variation rather than a universal.

**Moral rightness and justice are present in all languages but organized differently.** All eight languages have vocabulary for moral rightness, justice, or fairness that is related to but distinct from factual truth vocabulary. However, the degree of integration varies considerably. Turkish hak- merges rights, justice, truth, and religious reference into a single root with extensive derivational elaboration. Georgian mart'l- similarly spans correctness, moral rightness, and legal justice. By contrast, Yoruba keeps òdodo (justice/righteousness) more separate from tọ́ (correct), and Korean maintains a clear distinction between 정당하다 (legitimate) and 맞다 (correct). The merger of factual correctness with moral rightness within a single root is a feature of some languages (Georgian, Turkish, Basque zuzen-) but not others (Yoruba, Korean, Finnish).

**Discourse markers derived from truth-domain roots appear in all eight languages.** Georgian მართლაც, Yoruba nitootọ́, Finnish sebenarnya/totta puhuen, Basque benetan, Tamil uṇmaiyil, Indonesian sebenarnya, Turkish gerçekten, and Korean 사실은/솔직히 all function as grammaticalized discourse markers introducing corrections, frank statements, or factual clarifications. This grammaticalization pattern is cross-linguistically robust and appears to be a general tendency rather than a contact phenomenon.

**Reliability and credibility form a distinct cluster in all languages.** Every language has vocabulary for evaluating whether sources, persons, or information can be trusted, and this cluster is consistently kept separate from vocabulary for evaluating the truth-value of specific statements. Georgian სანდო (reliable) vs. საეჭვო (doubtful); Yoruba dájú (certain) and gbàgbọ́ (believe); Finnish luotettava (reliable) and uskottava (credible); Basque fidagarria (reliable) and zalantzagarria (doubtful); Tamil nampakam (reliability) and cantēkam (doubt); Indonesian güvenilir (reliable) and şüpheli (doubtful); Turkish güvenilir and şüpheli; Korean 신빙성 (credibility). The reliability cluster is consistently gradable (credibility can be high or low) in contrast to core truth predicates, which resist degree modification in several languages.

---

### Where Languages Split More Finely

**Tamil splits the truth-action domain most finely.** Tamil distinguishes speech acts of truth-telling (Group 1: uṇmaiyai col), concealment and revelation (Group 2: uṇmaiyai maṟai/veḷippaṭuttu), epistemic pursuit (Group 3: uṇmaiyai tēṭu), and acceptance of truth (Group 4: uṇmaiyai ēṟṟu) as separate groupings. Other languages have vocabulary for these distinctions but do not organize them into as many separate clusters. This fine-grained splitting may reflect the extensive verb+object collocation system in Tamil, where the same noun (uṇmai) combines with different verbs to create distinct semantic groups.

**Yoruba splits investigation and verification into more sub-groups than other languages.** Yoruba's F3 analysis identifies separate groups for investigation/verification processes, explanation/clarification, record/documentation, and evidence/demonstration — all built from the productive ṣe + noun construction. Other languages have vocabulary in these areas but do not show the same degree of lexical differentiation. This may reflect the productivity of the ṣe construction in Yoruba, which generates a large number of distinct action-denoting expressions.

**Finnish splits deception and distortion into separate groups.** Finnish distinguishes deliberate deception (Group 4: valhe, valehdella, petollinen) from distortion and misrepresentation (Group 12: vääristää, vääristely, harhaanjohtava). The distinction is between creating false representations (lying, forging) and corrupting existing true representations (distorting, misrepresenting). Other languages have vocabulary for both but do not consistently organize them into separate groups.

**Korean splits practical reality into a large independent cluster.** Korean's 실- (sil-) compounds form a distinct group (Group 8) covering actual practice, implementation, real-world application, and concrete results, with no clear parallel in other languages at this level of elaboration. The distinction between 실제 (actual reality) and 진실 (truth of statements) is maintained more explicitly in Korean than in most other languages.

---

### Where Languages Merge Distinctions

**Indonesian merges the most dimensions within the appropriateness/suitability group.** Indonesian Group 7 combines cocok (matching/compatible), wajar (reasonable/natural), pantas (appropriate/proper/deserved), tepat (precise/exact/appropriate), and pas (exact fit) into a single group. Other languages keep some of these distinctions separate: Yoruba has a dedicated appropriateness group (yẹ) distinct from its correspondence group (bá mu); Basque keeps egokia (appropriate) separate from berdina (same/equal); Finnish keeps appropriateness terms (oikea-aikainen) peripheral. Indonesian's merger may reflect the broad semantic range of the benar root, which licenses a wide range of correctness-related evaluations.

**Turkish merges reality, genuineness, and naturalness into a single group.** Turkish Group 2 combines gerçek (real/genuine), asıl (original/essential), özgün (authentic/original), taklit (imitation), doğal (natural), and yapay (artificial) into a single authenticity/reality assessment group. Other languages tend to keep the natural/artificial distinction (Finnish bunebrivi/khelovnuri; Georgian ბუნებრივი/ხელოვნური) somewhat separate from the genuine/counterfeit distinction. Turkish's merger may reflect the semantic range of gerçek, which covers both "real" (as opposed to imaginary) and "genuine" (as opposed to fake).

**Georgian merges sincerity and emotional genuineness with authenticity.** Georgian's F3 analysis identifies a separate group for sincerity and emotional genuineness (Group 4: გულწრფელი, ლიცემერი) that overlaps with the authenticity group. Other languages have vocabulary for sincerity (Finnish vilpitön, Turkish dürüst, Korean 진심) but tend to treat it as part of the honest character group rather than as a separate cluster. Georgian's separation may reflect the productivity of the გულ- (heart) root in sincerity expressions.

---

### Cases Where a Language Lacks a Clear Lexical Contrast Found Elsewhere

**Yoruba lacks a dedicated lexical antonym for gidi (genuine).** While all other languages have a clear lexical pair for genuine vs. fake (Georgian ნამდვილი/ყალბი, Finnish aito/väärennös, Basque benetakoa/faltsua, Tamil acal/pōli, Indonesian asli/palsu, Turkish gerçek/sahte, Korean 진짜/가짜), Yoruba expresses inauthenticity through negation (kì í ṣe gidi "it is not genuine") rather than a dedicated lexical item. This is the clearest case of an asymmetric lexicalization in the authenticity domain.

**Korean lacks a productive inchoative for propositional truth change.** While all other languages have some way to express "becoming true" or "becoming false" for propositions (Georgian გახდა constructions, Yoruba di constructions, Finnish toteutua/osoittautua, Basque bihurtu, Tamil āku, Indonesian menjadi, Turkish olmak/çıkmak), Korean treats truth as a static property that is discovered or revealed rather than something that changes. The constructions "진실이 되다" (become truth) and "거짓이 되다" (become false) are marginal or pragmatically restricted; Korean instead uses discovery verbs (드러나다, 밝혀지다). This is the most clearly documented case of a language-specific conceptual constraint on truth-domain constructions.

**Finnish lacks a common expression for "becoming untrue."** While Finnish has productive inchoative constructions for many truth-domain terms (toteutua "come true," todellistua "be realized"), it lacks a common expression for the reverse process — something that was true becoming false. The gap is documented explicitly in F6: "Finnish lacks specific verb for 'become suddenly false.'" Other languages handle this through discovery constructions (osoittautua vääräksi "turn out to be false") rather than a true inchoative. This parallels the Korean pattern but is less absolute.

**Tamil lacks dedicated vocabulary for objectivity/subjectivity.** While Georgian explicitly groups ობიექტური/სუბიექტური as a distinct semantic cluster, and other languages have borrowed these terms, Tamil's F3 analysis notes no dedicated group for objectivity/subjectivity. The distinction exists in Tamil (borrowed terms are available) but does not generate a distinct lexical cluster in the data.

**Indonesian and Korean lack a dedicated group for fiction vs. fact.** Georgian (Group 9: ფიქტიური vs. ნამდვილი ისტორია), Finnish (Group 15: tosielämä, tositarina), and Tamil (Group 16: uṇmai nikaḻvu, uṇmai katai) show dedicated vocabulary for distinguishing real events and true stories from fictional ones. Indonesian and Korean have relevant vocabulary (Indonesian tositarina-type expressions are absent; Korean 진짜 can be used) but do not show a distinct lexical cluster for this contrast.

**Basque lacks a dedicated group for epistemic certainty/probability.** While Yoruba (dájú, ìdájú), Finnish (todennäköinen, todennäköisyys), Tamil (uṟuti, cantēkam), Indonesian (kesin, şüpheli), Turkish (kesin, şüpheli), and Korean (확실하다, 불확실성) all show distinct vocabulary for epistemic certainty and probability, Basque's F3 analysis does not identify a separate group for this domain. Basque has ziurra (certain) and zalantzagarria (doubtful) but these are grouped under reliability/credibility rather than forming an independent epistemic certainty cluster.

---

### Distinguishing Well-Attested Cross-Language Patterns from Single-Language Observations

**Well-attested across six or more languages:**
- Lexical separation of deliberate lying from factual error (all eight languages)
- Agentive nominalization asymmetry: "liar" lexicalized, "truth-teller" not (documented in Georgian, Yoruba, Finnish, Tamil, Indonesian, Korean; implied in Basque and Turkish)
- Productive abstract nominalization from truth-domain adjectives (all eight languages)
- Discourse markers derived from truth-domain roots (all eight languages)
- Resistance to degree modification of core truth predicates (documented in Yoruba, Korean, Finnish, Basque, Tamil; implied in others)
- Separation of authenticity/genuineness from factual truth (all eight languages)
- Proverbial expressions asserting truth's ultimate triumph or difficulty (all eight languages)

**Attested in three to five languages:**
- Taste metaphors for truth and lies (Turkish, Yoruba, and implied in Korean's "white lie" calque)
- Absence of a simple verb meaning "to tell the truth" parallel to a dedicated "to lie" verb (Finnish, Yoruba, Korean, Tamil)
- Asymmetric lexicalization of negative compounds (Finnish, Indonesian; implied in others)
- Merger of factual correctness with moral rightness within a single root (Georgian, Turkish, Basque)

**Single-language observations:**
- Extension of "lie/false" to "futile/in vain" (Georgian ტყუილი only)
- Three-way register stratification of truth vocabulary (Tamil only)
- Advancement/progress group sharing morphology with truth terms (Korean 진/실 only)
- Objectivity/subjectivity as an explicitly grouped semantic cluster (Georgian F3 analysis only — may reflect analytical choice)
- Organizational management and live broadcasting as extensions of a correctness root (Basque zuzen- only)
- Elaborated rights/justice vocabulary as a major sub-domain of the truth field (Turkish hak- most extensively; Georgian mart'l-/samart'l- secondarily)
- Elaborated practical reality vs. theory cluster (Korean 실- compounds most extensively)
- Elaborated correspondence/matching cluster (Yoruba bá mu/ìbámu/jọ most extensively)

# G3 — Emergent Cross-Language Semantic Dimensions

---

## 1. Methodology

The dimensions below are inferred from patterns that recur across the F3 semantic grouping tables and are supported by F1 vocabulary distributions and F2 derivational evidence. Each dimension is defined by what the data shows: which terms cluster together, which contrasts are lexicalized, and which groupings appear independently in multiple languages. No dimension is proposed unless it is supported by evidence from at least two languages. Single-language observations are noted as such.

---

## 2. Proposed Dimensions

---

### Dimension 1: Propositional Correspondence

**Definition.** This dimension distinguishes terms used to evaluate whether statements, claims, or representations correspond to actual states of affairs from terms used for other purposes. It is the most basic truth-evaluation dimension in the data: terms in this cluster are applied to propositions, assertions, or information, and their primary function is to mark whether content matches reality. It is distinct from evaluations of objects (authenticity), persons (honesty), or actions (moral rightness).

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: სიმართლე (simart'le) "truth," სწორი (sts'ori) "correct," მცდარი (mts'dari) "erroneous," ჭეშმარიტი (ch'eshmarit'i) "true"
- Yoruba: òtítọ́ "truth," tọ́ "to be correct," irọ́ "lie," kò tọ́ "to be incorrect"
- Finnish: tosi "true," totuus "truth," väärä "wrong/false," paikkansapitävä "accurate"
- Basque: egia "truth," egiazkoa "true," gezurra "lie," gezurrezko "false"
- Tamil: uṇmai "truth," cari "correct," tappu "wrong," poy "lie/false"
- Indonesian: benar "true/correct," salah "wrong," sah "valid"
- Turkish: doğru "true/correct," yanlış "wrong/false," gerçek "real/true"
- Korean: 진실 (jinsil) "truth," 사실 (sasil) "fact," 맞다 (matda) "correct," 틀리다 (teullida) "wrong"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. This is the most robustly attested dimension in the dataset. In all languages it forms the core of the truth-domain vocabulary and generates the most productive derivational families. In several languages (Georgian, Turkish, Basque) this dimension partially merges with moral rightness (Dimension 5); in others (Yoruba, Korean) it is kept more separate.

---

### Dimension 2: Deliberate Deception vs. Unintentional Error

**Definition.** This dimension distinguishes terms that mark intentional false representation or lying from terms that mark unintentional error or mistake. The deception terms consistently imply a speaker or agent who knows the truth and chooses to misrepresent it; the error terms imply incorrect belief or action without intent to deceive. The two clusters show different moral valence, different collocational patterns, and different derivational behavior across languages.

**Representative terms (deception side):**
- Georgian: ტყუილი (t'q'uili) "lie," მოტყუება (mot'q'ueba) "deception," მატყუარა (mat'q'uara) "liar"
- Yoruba: irọ́ "lie," purọ́ "to lie," apurọ́ "liar"
- Finnish: valhe "lie," valehdella "to lie," valehtelija "liar"
- Basque: gezurra "lie," gezurkeria "habitual lying," iruzurra "fraud"
- Tamil: poy "lie," poy col "tell lies," poyyar "liars"
- Indonesian: bohong "lie/to lie," pembohong "liar," kebohongan "falsehood"
- Turkish: yalan "lie," yalancı "liar," yalanlamak "to deny/refute"
- Korean: 거짓말 (geojinmal) "lie," 거짓말쟁이 (geojinmaljjaengi) "liar," 허위 (heowi) "falsehood"

**Representative terms (unintentional error side):**
- Georgian: მცდარი (mts'dari) "erroneous," შეცდომა (shets'doma) "mistake"
- Yoruba: àṣìṣe "error, mistake," ṣìṣe "to err"
- Finnish: virheellinen "erroneous," väärinkäsitys "misunderstanding"
- Basque: okerra "wrong/erroneous," okertu "to go wrong"
- Tamil: tappu "mistake," tavaṟu "error"
- Indonesian: keliru "mistaken," kesalahan "error/mistake"
- Turkish: hatalı "erroneous," hata "error," yanılmak "to be mistaken"
- Korean: 틀리다 (teullida) "to be wrong/incorrect," 실수 (silsu) "mistake"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. The deception terms consistently carry stronger moral valence and generate more agentive nominalizations (liar-words). The error terms tend to be softer and more neutral. In several languages (Georgian, Finnish, Indonesian) the two clusters are explicitly separated in F3 analyses. The distinction is maintained even when a single root covers both domains (e.g., Georgian ყალბი q'albi covers both "fake" and "forged," but the deliberate deception implication is present).

---

### Dimension 3: Authenticity of Objects and Representations

**Definition.** This dimension covers terms used to evaluate whether physical objects, documents, artworks, products, or identities are genuine originals versus counterfeits, forgeries, or imitations. It is distinct from propositional correspondence (Dimension 1) in that it applies to objects rather than statements, and from deliberate deception (Dimension 2) in that it focuses on the status of the object rather than the intent of an agent. The contrast is between "the real thing" and "a copy or fake."

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: ნამდვილი (namdvili) "genuine/real," ყალბი (q'albi) "fake/counterfeit," ავთენტური (avt'ent'uri) "authentic"
- Yoruba: gidi "genuine/real," wúrà gidi "genuine gold"
- Finnish: aito "genuine/authentic," aitous "genuineness," väärennös "forgery"
- Basque: benetakoa "genuine/real," faltsua "false/fake," faltsutu "to falsify/forge"
- Tamil: acal "original/genuine," pōli "fake/counterfeit," pōliyāṉa "fake"
- Indonesian: asli "genuine/authentic," palsu "fake/counterfeit," pemalsuan "forgery"
- Turkish: gerçek "real/genuine," sahte "fake/counterfeit," sahtekâr "forger/fraud"
- Korean: 진짜 (jinjja) "real/genuine," 가짜 (gajja) "fake/counterfeit," 진본 (jinbon) "authentic original," 모조품 (mojopum) "imitation product"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. In most languages this dimension is kept distinct from propositional truth, though some terms participate in both (Georgian ნამდვილი, Tamil uṇmai, Turkish gerçek). The negative pole (fake/counterfeit) tends to be more lexically elaborated than the positive pole in several languages. Yoruba is the only language where the negative pole lacks a dedicated lexical item (inauthenticity is expressed through negation of gidi rather than a separate word).

---

### Dimension 4: Honesty and Moral Character

**Definition.** This dimension covers terms that evaluate the truthfulness, integrity, or sincerity of persons as a stable character trait or disposition, rather than evaluating specific statements or objects. Terms in this cluster are applied to persons or their habitual conduct and imply a moral assessment of character. They are distinct from propositional truth (which evaluates statements) and from deliberate deception (which evaluates specific acts).

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: გულწრფელი (gults'rpeli) "sincere/honest," ლიცემერი (lits'emeri) "hypocritical," ნეიმარი (nērmai) — not Georgian; see below
- Yoruba: ìwà rere "good character," ìwà búburú "bad character," ọmọ òtítọ́ "truthful person," ọkàn tọ́ "straight heart"
- Finnish: rehellinen "honest," vilpitön "sincere," dürüst — not Finnish; see below
- Basque: zintzoa "honest/sincere," zintzotasuna "honesty/integrity," zintzoki "honestly"
- Tamil: nērmai "honesty/integrity," nērmaiyāṉa "honest," nērmaikku māṟāṉa "contrary to honesty"
- Indonesian: jujur "honest/truthful," kejujuran "honesty," dürüst — not Indonesian; see below
- Turkish: dürüst "honest/truthful," dürüstlük "honesty/integrity," dürüstçe "honestly"
- Korean: 정직 (jeongjik) "honesty/integrity," 솔직 (soljik) "frankness/candor," 진심 (jinsim) "sincerity"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. In most languages this dimension forms a distinct cluster in F3 analyses. The distinction between honesty as a character trait (this dimension) and truthfulness of specific statements (Dimension 1) is maintained across languages, though some terms participate in both. Sincerity of emotional expression (e.g., Georgian გულწრფელი, Korean 진심) is sometimes grouped with this dimension and sometimes treated as a sub-dimension of authenticity.

---

### Dimension 5: Moral Rightness and Justice

**Definition.** This dimension covers terms that evaluate actions, decisions, or situations according to moral or legal standards of rightness, fairness, and justice. It is distinct from propositional truth (which evaluates statements) and from honesty (which evaluates character). Terms in this cluster are applied to actions, decisions, social arrangements, or legal outcomes and imply normative evaluation according to standards of what is right or fair.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: სამართლიანი (samart'liani) "just/fair," მართლმსაჯულება (mart'lmsajuleba) "justice/jurisprudence," უსამართლობა (usamart'loba) "injustice"
- Yoruba: òdodo "justice/righteousness," ṣe òdodo "to do justice," ìwà rere "good character/conduct"
- Finnish: oikeudenmukaisuus "justice/fairness," oikeutettu "justified/warranted," oikeuttaa "to justify"
- Basque: zuzentasuna "correctness/justice/rectitude," zuzenbide "law/jurisprudence," zintzoa "honest/upright"
- Tamil: niyāyam "justice/fairness," aṟam "virtue/righteousness/dharma," nīti "justice/righteousness"
- Indonesian: adil "just/fair," keadilan — not in P1 data; pantas "appropriate/deserved"
- Turkish: hak "right/justice," haklı "justified/in the right," haksız "unjust," adil "just/fair," adalet "justice"
- Korean: 정당하다 (jeongdanghada) "legitimate/justified," 타당하다 (tadanghada) "valid/reasonable"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, but the degree of integration with propositional truth varies considerably. Turkish (hak-) and Georgian (mart'l-/samart'l-) show the strongest merger of moral rightness with factual correctness within a single root. Yoruba, Korean, and Finnish keep this dimension more separate from propositional truth. In Basque, zuzen- merges correctness, moral rightness, and legal concepts. The dimension is present everywhere but its lexical organization relative to Dimension 1 is a major point of cross-language variation.

---

### Dimension 6: Reliability and Credibility of Sources

**Definition.** This dimension covers terms used to evaluate whether sources, persons, or information can be trusted or relied upon, independently of whether their specific claims have been verified. It is distinct from propositional truth (which evaluates whether claims are true) and from honesty (which evaluates character). Terms in this cluster are applied to sources, witnesses, or information and assess their trustworthiness or believability as a property that precedes or enables verification.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: სანდო (sando) "reliable/trustworthy," საეჭვო (saech'vo) "doubtful/dubious," დამაჯერებელი (damajerebeli) "convincing/credible"
- Yoruba: dájú "certain/sure," gbàgbọ́ "to believe/trust," ìgbàgbọ́ "belief/faith/trust"
- Finnish: luotettava "reliable/trustworthy," uskottava "believable/credible," luotettavuus "reliability"
- Basque: fidagarria "reliable/trustworthy," sinesgarria "believable/credible," zalantzagarria "doubtful/dubious"
- Tamil: nampakam "reliability/trustworthiness," nampikkai "trust/belief/faith," cantēkam "doubt/suspicion"
- Indonesian: güvenilir — not Indonesian; see below; sah "valid" (partially overlaps)
- Turkish: güvenilir "reliable/trustworthy," güvenilirlik "reliability," inandırıcı "convincing/credible"
- Korean: 신빙성 (sinbingseong) "credibility/reliability," 그럴듯하다 (geureoldeuthada) "plausible"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. This dimension consistently forms a distinct cluster in F3 analyses and is consistently kept separate from propositional truth. A key feature across languages is that reliability terms are gradable (credibility can be high or low, can increase or decrease) while core truth predicates resist degree modification in several languages. The distinction between "this source is reliable" and "this claim is true" is maintained across all eight languages.

---

### Dimension 7: Epistemic Certainty and Doubt

**Definition.** This dimension covers terms that express the degree of confidence or certainty a speaker has regarding a claim, independently of whether the claim is actually true. Terms in this cluster mark epistemic stance — how sure the speaker is — rather than the truth-value of the proposition itself. They are distinct from reliability (which evaluates sources) and from propositional truth (which evaluates content).

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: ეჭვი (ech'vi) "doubt/suspicion," საეჭვო (saech'vo) "doubtful," უტყუარი (ut'q'uari) "infallible/certain"
- Yoruba: ìdájú "certainty/assurance," dájú "to be certain," dájúdájú "very certain"
- Finnish: todennäköinen "probable/likely," todennäköisyys "probability," epätodennäköinen "improbable"
- Basque: ziurra "certain/sure," ziurtasuna "certainty," zalantzagarria "doubtful"
- Tamil: uṟuti "certainty/confirmation," cantēkam "doubt/suspicion," teḷivu "clarity"
- Indonesian: kesin — not Indonesian; see below; şüpheli — not Indonesian; see below
- Turkish: kesin "certain/definite," kesinlik "certainty," şüpheli "doubtful/suspicious," kuşkulu "doubtful"
- Korean: 확실하다 (hwaksilhada) "certain/sure," 불확실성 (bulhwaksilseong) "uncertainty," 명백하다 (myeongbaekhada) "obvious/clear"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, but the degree to which it forms a distinct cluster varies. Finnish, Turkish, and Korean show the most elaborated epistemic certainty vocabulary. Basque groups certainty terms under reliability rather than as a separate cluster. Yoruba's certainty terms (dájú) are closely linked to verification processes. The dimension is present everywhere but its independence from Dimension 6 (reliability) varies across languages.

---

### Dimension 8: Appearance vs. Underlying Reality

**Definition.** This dimension covers terms that distinguish how things appear or seem from how they actually are. Terms in this cluster are used when surface appearances may be misleading or when the underlying reality differs from what is manifest. It is distinct from propositional truth (which evaluates statements) and from authenticity (which evaluates objects) in that it focuses on the gap between surface and depth, or between seeming and being.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: მოჩვენებითი (moch'venebiti) "apparent/seeming," ზედაპირული (zedap'iruli) "superficial," არსებითი (arsebiti) "essential/substantial," ნამდვილი სახე (namdvili sakhe) "true face/real nature"
- Yoruba: ẹnu ń sọ, ọkàn ò mọ̀ "mouth speaks but heart doesn't know" (proverbial)
- Finnish: todellinen "real/actual" (vs. apparent), harhaanjohtava "misleading," petollinen "deceptive"
- Basque: itxurazko "apparent/seeming/ostensible," ageria "evident/manifest," funtsean "fundamentally/essentially," benetakoa "genuine/real"
- Tamil: uṇmai mukam "true face," poy mukam "false face," māyai "illusion/deception," iyal pu "natural state/essence"
- Indonesian: sebenarnya "actually/in truth," hakikat "essence/true nature," nyata "real/actual"
- Turkish: gerçek yüz "true face/real nature," gerçeğe aykırı "contrary to reality," gerçekdışı "unreal/unrealistic"
- Korean: 진면목 (jinmyeonmok) "true character/real nature," 실체 (silche) "substance/entity/reality," 본질 (bonjil) "essence/nature"

**Distribution.** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, but the degree of elaboration varies. Georgian, Basque, and Turkish show the most systematic vocabulary for this dimension. Tamil and Korean show it primarily through metaphorical expressions (true face/false face). Finnish and Indonesian show it through adverbial discourse markers (sebenarnya, tosiasiassa). The dimension is present everywhere but is more elaborated in some languages than others.

---

### Dimension 9: Validity and Legitimacy

**Definition.** This dimension covers terms that evaluate whether actions, documents, arguments, or statuses conform to established rules, legal requirements, or accepted standards — whether they "count" as valid or legitimate. It is distinct from moral rightness (which evaluates ethical quality) and from propositional truth (which evaluates factual content). Terms in this cluster are applied in legal, administrative, logical, and procedural contexts.

## 4. Assessment of Dimensions

### Strongly Supported Cross-Linguistically

The following dimensions are supported by clearly lexicalized evidence from all eight languages and form distinct clusters in F3 analyses across multiple languages:

- **D1 (Propositional Correspondence)** — universal, core of the truth domain in every language
- **D2 (Deliberate Deception vs. Unintentional Error)** — universal, with consistent moral valence asymmetry
- **D3 (Authenticity of Objects)** — universal, though yo lacks a lexical antonym for gidi
- **D4 (Honesty and Moral Character)** — universal, consistently distinct from D1
- **D5 (Moral Rightness and Justice)** — universal, though degree of merger with D1 varies
- **D6 (Reliability and Credibility)** — universal, consistently gradable unlike core truth predicates
- **D7 (Epistemic Certainty and Doubt)** — universal, though independence from D6 varies
- **D12 (Verification and Proof Processes)** — universal, with varying internal organization
- **D13 (Discourse Marking of Truth Stance)** — universal, emerging from grammaticalization pattern

### Moderately Supported (Present in All Languages but Unevenly Elaborated)

- **D8 (Appearance vs. Underlying Reality)** — present in all 8 languages but degree of systematic elaboration varies considerably; ka, eu, tr most systematic; yo primarily proverbial
- **D9 (Validity and Legitimacy)** — present in all 8 languages but degree of independence from D5 varies; id and tr most elaborated
- **D10 (Similarity and Correspondence)** — present in all 8 languages but forms a distinct F3 cluster only in ka, yo, eu, id; yo most elaborated
- **D11 (Practical Reality vs. Theory/Nominal Status)** — present in all 8 languages but very uneven elaboration; ko most extensive, fi distinct cluster, others less systematic

### Dimensions That Split, Merge, or Vary Across Languages

**D1 and D5 merge in ka, tr, eu:** The mart'l- root (ka), hak- root (tr), and zuzen- root (eu) each span both propositional correctness and moral rightness within a single derivational family. In yo, ko, and fi these dimensions are kept more separate.

**D6 and D7 merge in eu:** Basque groups certainty terms (ziurra) under reliability/credibility rather than forming an independent epistemic certainty cluster. In fi, tr, and ko these dimensions are more clearly separated.

**D3 and D1 partially merge in ka and tr:** Georgian ნამდვილი (namdvili) and Turkish gerçek participate in both authenticity of objects and propositional truth contexts. In fi (aito vs. tosi) and yo (gidi vs. tọ́) these dimensions are kept more separate.

**D4 and D3 partially merge in ka:** Georgian გულწრფელი (sincere) is grouped with emotional genuineness in a way that bridges honesty of character and authenticity of feeling. Other languages tend to group sincerity more clearly with D4.

**D9 and D5 partially merge in ka, eu:** Georgian and Basque legal/validity vocabulary is closely integrated with the correctness/justice root. In id and tr these dimensions are more clearly separated.

**D11 is most elaborated in ko:** Korean's 실- cluster represents the most extensive development of the practical reality vs. theory dimension in the dataset. This is a single-language elaboration rather than a cross-linguistic pattern, though the dimension itself is present everywhere.

**D10 is most elaborated in yo:** Yoruba's bá mu/ìbámu/jọ/ìjọra cluster represents the most extensive development of the correspondence/matching dimension. This is a single-language elaboration.

**D2 shows a consistent agentive asymmetry across languages:** The "liar" agentive is lexicalized in all 8 languages; the "truth-teller" agentive is absent or requires periphrastic expression in at least 6 languages. This asymmetry is a cross-linguistically robust pattern within D2.

**Core truth predicates resist degree modification in yo, ko, fi, eu, ta:** Multiple languages treat truth as categorical rather than scalar, which constrains the constructional behavior of D1 terms. This constraint is not universal (ka, id, tr show more gradable uses) but is attested in enough languages to be noted as a recurring pattern.

| Factual Correctness and Accuracy | This group includes terms used to evaluate whether statements, information, or answers correspond to facts or reality, particularly in contexts where precision and correctness can be objectively verified. These terms are commonly used in educational, technical, and informational contexts to distinguish correct from incorrect information, and often appear in contexts involving verification, measurement, or testing. | სწორი (sts'ori) — "correct, right, proper"; მართალი (mart'ali) — "right, correct" (when evaluating factual claims); ზუსტი (zusti) — "precise, exact, accurate"; მცდარი (mts'dari) — "erroneous, mistaken, false"; სწორი პასუხი (sts'ori p'asukhi) — "correct answer"; ზუსტი ინფორმაცია (zusti inpormatsia) — "accurate information"; მცდარი ინფორმაცია (mts'dari inpormatsia) — "false information"; შეცდომა (shets'doma) — "mistake, error"; გასწორება (gasts'oreba) — "correction, rectification"; სიზუსტე (sizuste) — "precision, exactness" | მართალი (mart'ali) — overlaps with moral/justice domain when describing persons rather than statements; ადეკვატური (adek'vat'uri) — can evaluate both factual accuracy and appropriateness | |
| Authenticity and Genuineness | This group contains terms that distinguish real, original, or genuine things from fake, counterfeit, or artificial ones. These terms are particularly common in contexts involving material objects, documents, cultural artifacts, personal identity, and emotional sincerity. The focus is on whether something is what it claims or appears to be, rather than on factual correctness of statements. | ნამდვილი (namdvili) — "real, genuine, authentic"; ყალბი (q'albi) — "false, fake, counterfeit"; ავთენტური (avt'ent'uri) — "authentic, genuine"; ბუნებრივი (bunebrivi) — "natural, genuine"; ხელოვნური (khelovnuri) — "artificial, man-made"; ნაღდი (naghdi) — "real, genuine" (metaphorical use); ნამდვილი მეგობარი (namdvili megobari) — "true friend"; ყალბი ფული (q'albi puli) — "counterfeit money"; გაყალბება (gaq'albeba) — "falsification, counterfeiting"; ნამდვილობა (namdviloba) — "reality, genuineness, authenticity"; ავთენტური ნამუშევარი (avt'ent'uri namushevarი) — "authentic work"; ბუნებრივი ქცევა (bunebrivi ktseva) — "natural behavior, genuine behavior" | ჭეშმარიტი (ch'eshmarit'i) — can describe both authentic things and true statements; რეალური (realuri) — overlaps with existence/actuality domain | |

| àfihàn (demonstration) + ṣe (to do) | Mo ṣe àfihàn | mo ṣe àfihàn | I demonstrated / I showed / I proved | Construction for demonstrating or proving. Common in argumentative and evidential contexts. | [CORE] |

| tọ́ (to be straight) + lọ́nà (on the path) | Ó tọ́ lọ́nà | ó tọ́ lọ́nà | He/she is on the right path / is doing the right thing | Metaphorical construction evaluating moral conduct or correct procedure. Common in moral discourse. | [CORE] |

| ọ̀rọ̀ (word) + òfo (empty/vain) | Ọ̀rọ̀ òfo ni | ọ̀rọ̀ òfo ni | It is an empty word / a vain statement | Construction dismissing statements as meaningless or false. Common in critical discourse. | [CORE] |
| ìdí (reason) + ṣe (to be) | Ó ṣe ìdí | ó ṣe ìdí | It is the reason / It is the cause | Construction identifying reasons or causes. Common in explanatory contexts. | [CORE] |

| tọ́ (to be correct) + títí (completely) | Ó tọ́ títí | ó tọ́ títí | It is completely correct / absolutely right | Construction emphasizing total correctness. Common for strong confirmation. | [CORE] |

| Epistemic Certainty and Belief | This group includes expressions used to indicate the degree of confidence, certainty, or belief that a speaker has regarding claims or propositions. | Possibility and Feasibility | This group includes expressions used to evaluate whether something can occur, be done, or be accomplished. | Importance and Significance | This group contains expressions used to evaluate the weight, relevance, or significance of matters, statements, or situations. | Speech Acts and Assertion | This group includes expressions used when making statements, telling, speaking, or asserting things. These terms focus on the act of communication itself and the manner in which information is conveyed. These terms refer to systematic processes of discovering or confirming truth rather than the truth itself. | Explanation and Clarification | This group includes expressions used when explaining, clarifying, describing, or making things understandable. These terms focus on making information clear or comprehensible rather than establishing its truth. They appear in educational, communicative, and interpretive contexts. | ṣe àlàyé (to explain, to clarify), ṣe àpèjúwe (to describe, to depict), ṣe àpẹẹrẹ (to give an example), àtọ́kùn (explanation, clarification), ṣe àtọ́kùn (to clarify, to explain) | ṣe àfihàn (to demonstrate) — overlaps with evidence/proof; ṣe é mọ̀ (to be clear) — state rather than process | ṣe àpẹẹrẹ (to give example) overlaps with explanation |
| Record and Documentation | This group contains expressions used for recording, documenting, correcting, or preserving information. These terms refer to activities of creating and maintaining accurate records rather than evaluating truth directly. They appear in administrative, archival, and editorial contexts. | ṣe àkọsílẹ̀ (to record, to document), ṣe àtúnṣe (to correct, to revise), àṣìṣe (error, mistake), ṣe àṣìṣe (to make an error) | ìwé tọ́ (correct document) — evaluates accuracy of records; ṣìṣe (to err) — making errors rather than correcting them | |
| Evidence and Demonstration | This group includes expressions used when providing evidence, showing proof, or demonstrating claims. These terms focus on the presentation of support for assertions rather than the assertions themselves. They appear in argumentative, legal, and evidential contexts. | ṣe àfihàn (to demonstrate, to show, to prove), ṣe àmì (to be a sign, to serve as evidence), ẹ̀rí (evidence, witness), jẹ́rìí (testimony, witness), ṣe ìjẹ́rìí (to bear witness, to testify) | fi òtítọ́ hàn (to reveal the truth) — overlaps with investigation; ṣe àpẹẹrẹ (to give example) — overlaps with explanation | ṣe àfihàn (to demonstrate) overlaps with evidence/proof; fi òtítọ́ hàn (to reveal the truth) overlaps with investigation; ṣe àpẹẹrẹ (to give example) overlaps with explanation |
| Proverbial and Idiomatic Expressions | This group contains conventionalized sayings, proverbs, and idiomatic expressions related to truth and falsehood. #### F4_construction_table
# CLCA Protocol v3.4 — F4 Construction Table
# Language: Yoruba (yo)

| Construction Type | Example | Transliteration | Translation | Usage Notes | Epistemic Status |
|------------------|---------|-----------------|-------------|-------------|------------------|
| Subject + tọ́ | Ọ̀rọ̀ náà tọ́ | ọ̀rọ̀ náà tọ́ | That statement is true/correct | Most natural and frequent pattern for asserting correctness/truth. Used in everyday speech for statements, claims, and factual assertions. No register restrictions. | [CORE] |
| Subject + jẹ́ + òtítọ́ | (implied in notes) | — | — | Standard nominal predicate construction. Used when emphasizing truth as a quality or essence rather than simple correctness. Common in formal and informal contexts. | [CORE] |
| Subject + jẹ́ + irọ́ | Ìròyìn yìí jẹ́ irọ́ | ìròyìn yìí jẹ́ irọ́ | This news is a lie | Primary pattern for identifying something as false/a lie. The nominal irọ́ requires copula jẹ́. Very common in everyday discourse. | [CORE] |
| Subject + purọ́ | (implied in notes) | — | — | Intransitive verb for "to lie/be false." Used for active lying or falsehood. Common in both formal and informal speech. | [CORE] |
| Subject + ṣe òtítọ́ | (alternate construction) | — | — | Light verb construction, less common than jẹ́ òtítọ́ | [CORE] |
| Subject + jẹ́ + òdodo | (alternate construction) | — | — | Alternative lexical item for truthfulness | [CORE] |
| Subject + kò + tọ́ | Ọ̀rọ̀ náà kò tọ́ | ọ̀rọ̀ náà kò tọ́ | That statement is not true/correct | Standard negation pattern. Most natural way to deny correctness or truth. Used across all registers without restriction. | [CORE] |
| Subject + kò + jẹ́ + òtítọ́ | Èyí kò jẹ́ òtítọ́ | èyí kò jẹ́ òtítọ́ | This is not the truth | Standard negation of nominal predicate. Emphasizes that something fails to be truth itself. Common in formal and informal contexts. | [CORE] |
| kò + tọ́ + rárá | (implied in notes) | — | — | Emphatic negation adding "at all." Very common in spoken Yoruba for strong denial. The particle rárá intensifies the negation. | [CORE] |
| Subject + kò + purọ́ | (alternate construction) | — | — | Less common as double negative implication | [CORE] |
| Subject + kì í ṣe + òtítọ́ | (alternate construction) | — | — | Emphatic negative copula construction | [CORE] |
| Noun + tọ́ | ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́ | ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́ | true word, correct statement | Most productive pattern for modifying nouns with truth/correctness. Functions as headless relative clause. Used across all registers. | [CORE] |
| Noun + òtítọ́ | ẹ̀rí òtítọ́ | ẹ̀rí òtítọ́ | truthful evidence, true testimony | Noun-noun compound/juxtaposition. Common with abstract nouns like ẹ̀rí (evidence/testimony). The modifier òtítọ́ follows the head noun. | [CORE] |
| Noun + gidi | (implied in notes) | — | — | Adjective gidi (genuine, real) can modify truth-related nouns but is less specific to truth domain. More general authenticity marker. | [MARGINAL] |
| Noun + òdodo | (alternate construction) | — | — | Alternative modifier emphasizing honesty | [CORE] |
| Noun + tí ó tọ́ | (alternate construction) | — | — | Full relative clause, more explicit but less common | [CORE] |
| Subject + di + òtítọ́ | Ọ̀rọ̀ náà di òtítọ́ | ọ̀rọ̀ náà di òtítọ́ | That matter became the truth / turned out to be true | Used for discovery or revelation rather than change in truth-value. Not common for statements "becoming true" as truth is treated as static property. Context-dependent usage. Yoruba conceptualizes truth as inherent rather than emergent. The di construction is pragmatically marked and typically implies that something was revealed to be true rather than changed from false to true. More common in narrative contexts describing discovery. | [MARGINAL] |
| Subject + hàn + bí òtítọ́ | (alternate construction) | — | — | Revelation/appearance construction | [CORE] |
| A rí i pé ó tọ́ | (alternate construction) | — | — | Evidential construction, more common than inchoative | [CORE] |
| Subject + mú + kí + Clause | Ó mú kí ọ̀rọ̀ náà tọ́ | ó mú kí ọ̀rọ̀ náà tọ́ | He/she made that statement true / verified it | Periphrastic causative. Pragmatically marked; implies verification or making something correspond to truth rather than creating truth. Uncommon in everyday speech. Yoruba lacks morphological causative for truth predicates. The mú kí pattern is conceptually odd for truth (one cannot "make" truth), so it's reinterpreted as verification. | [MARGINAL] |
| Subject + jẹ́ + kí + Clause | Ó jẹ́ kí n sọ òtítọ́ | ó jẹ́ kí n sọ òtítọ́ | He/she allowed me to tell the truth | Permissive causative. Common construction for allowing/enabling truth-telling. Used across registers. More natural than mú kí for truth domain. The jẹ́ kí pattern is more natural as it expresses permission/enablement. | [CORE] |
| Subject + ṣe + kí + Clause | (alternate construction) | — | — | Alternative causative verb, similar restrictions | [MARGINAL] |
| Subject + fún + Object + láyè + láti + Verb | (alternate construction) | — | — | More explicit permissive | [CORE] |
| ò- + tí + Verb | òtítọ́ | òtítọ́ | truth, truthfulness | Lexicalized nominalization from tọ́. This specific form is the standard word for "truth." Not productive as a pattern—òtítọ́ is a fixed lexical item. | [CORE] |
| ì- + Verb | ìgbàgbọ́ | ìgbàgbọ́ | belief, faith | Highly productive prefix for creating abstract nouns from verbs. Used extensively in truth domain: ìmọ̀ (knowledge), ìdájú (certainty), ìbámu (correspondence). | [CORE] |
| àì- + Verb | àìtọ́, àìmọ̀ | — | incorrectness, ignorance | Productive negative nominalization prefix. Creates abstract nouns denoting absence or negation of the verbal property. Common in formal and philosophical discourse. | [CORE] |
| ìṣe + Noun | (alternate construction) | — | — | Periphrastic nominalization, less common | [CORE] |
| ọ̀nà + Verb | (alternate construction) | — | — | Manner nominalization, different semantic profile | [CORE] |
| a- + Verb | apurọ́ | apurọ́ | liar | Lexicalized agent noun from purọ́ (to lie). The a- prefix is not productive with tọ́ (*atọ́ is not attested). Used commonly for "liar." | [CORE] |
| ọmọ + Noun | ọmọ òtítọ́ | ọmọ òtítọ́ | truthful person, child of truth | Productive pattern using ọmọ (child/person of). Common way to express "truthful person" since *atọ́ doesn't exist. Used in both literal and metaphorical senses. | [CORE] |
| ẹni + Noun | (implied in notes) | — | — | More formal pattern using ẹni (person). Less common than ọmọ construction but used in formal or written contexts. | [MARGINAL] |
| ẹni tí ó + Verb | (alternate construction) | — | — | Relative clause construction, more explicit | [CORE] |
| oníṣe + Noun | (alternate construction) | — | — | Agentive with oní- prefix, less common for truth domain | [MARGINAL] |
| Verb + pé + Clause | Mo gbàgbọ́ pé ó tọ́ | mo gbàgbọ́ pé ó tọ́ | I believe that it is true | Standard declarative complementation. Used with verbs of saying, thinking, believing. The complementizer pé is obligatory. Very common across all registers. | [CORE] |
| Verb + bí + Clause | Mo mọ̀ bí ó ṣe tọ́ | mo mọ̀ bí ó ṣe tọ́ | I know how it is true / whether it is true | Interrogative/manner complementation. Used for embedded questions or manner descriptions. Common with epistemic verbs like mọ̀ (know). | [CORE] |
